newsitem.title: USA: Mayor says Washington "a good city getting better".
newsitem.headline: Mayor says Washington "a good city getting better".

text.p: Mayor Marion Barry, sounding like he plans to run for a fifth term, told Washington residents they are living in "a good city getting better" and not in a city depicted in the press as in deep distress.

Barry invited thousands of followers to historic Lincoln Theatre to hear a "State of the District" speech in which he ticked off the progress his administration has made in battling numbing problems of crime, poverty, trash collection, pot-holed streets, failing schools and near bankruptcy.
A campaign-like slogan, "A promise made. A promise kept. A good city getting better", was shouted repeatedly as he cited statistics to back his claim that the city is on an upswing.

Until Wednesday night's widely advertised speech, Barry, 61, has taken a back seat in recent months to a Congressionally appointed financial control board that has taken away much of his power to spend and tax.

The mayor served a prison term after a 1994 conviction for cocaine abuse and perjury in a sting operation during which federal agents videotaped him blaming a former lover for luring him to a hotel room. His "the bitch set me up" line made him fodder for jokes on television comedy shows.

But at home, Barry a former civil rights leader, enjoys deep support among the city's overwhelmingly black majority, despite his string of publicized battles with drugs, alcoholism and a one-time reputation as a lady's man.

Barry, who recently had prostate cancer surgery, has repeatedly declined to say whether he will run for a fifth term. Some political opponents call him "Mayor-for-life Marion" and say he will never quit.

In what sounded like a campaign kick-off speech, Barry covered all the bases, promising to clean the streets of crime, improve police morale, tow away scores of abandoned cars, fix broken bridges and schools and reform an ailing Medicare system that provides health care for the city's poor and elderly.

Defending the city's 30,000 workers, Barry said: "We are castigated, berated and stereotyped as bumbling, stumbling 'can't do anything right' workers." He said that there were some cases where that description fit but he would make them "shape up or ship out."

Some of Barry's rhetoric rang hollow. A consulting firm on Tuesday, for instance, found in a report that the 3,500 member police force was beset with "chronic" problems and worked at "minimum levels" and that city residents lived in fear.
